## Two kinds of aim {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to understand**

- What reproducibility, robustness and replicability each mean, and why they come apart
- Why analysts disagree – and how much of that is disagreement about the *question*
- What a causal graph is good for, in an experiment as much as in observational data
- What a multiverse shows, and what it cannot show
- What preregistration settles, and what it leaves open
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to be able to do**

- Get an analysis running from someone else's materials
- Write an estimand statement, and a causal graph that matches it
- Reproduce a published result exactly, and explain why it came out as it did
- Vary a specification one choice at a time and read what changed
- Preregister an analysis before you run it, and report where it sits among the alternatives
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Two columns, because the course has two kinds of aim. On the left is what I want you to understand, and most of it is conceptual work that has little to do with code. On the right is what I want you to be able to do, and every item there is something you will have done at least once with your own hands before we finish. If you take home only the left-hand column, you will have heard some interesting arguments and changed nothing about how you work. If you take home only the right-hand column, you will have learned some R. What I am after is the two together, because the concepts tell you which of the things you can now do is worth doing.
:::
